stories.headline: Russia hits Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine
stories.dek: Air raid sirens sounded after Friedrich Merz arrived, and a strike damaged the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River.
paragraphs: Russia struck a bridge in Kyiv on Sunday shortly after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived for a surprise visit. The attack damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge, city officials said. Merz came to show support as Germany and Ukraine moved toward a new military aid package.

Kyiv is split by the Dnipro River, and bridges are vital links between the east and west of the city. The Northern Bridge is one of several crossings hit in recent days. Air raid sirens sounded across the capital, and officials warned residents about approaching Russian attack drones.

It is not yet clear how badly the bridge was damaged or how long repairs will take. Officials have not said whether anyone was hurt in the strike. Merz and President Volodymyr Zelensky were expected to meet, but Germany has not yet announced the final terms of the aid deal.
stories.changes: For people in Kyiv, another key river crossing may face disruption while attacks continue during high-level foreign visits.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Kyiv has fallen or that Germany is entering the war directly.

cover.title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during German chancellor visit
cover.standfirst: Russia hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge on Sunday soon after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital under tight security. Air raid sirens sounded across the city. The visit was meant to show European backing as Berlin and Kyiv near a military aid package worth more than US$1 billion.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Top-down, the Dnipro runs vertically through the cover as a single black band, with the Northern Bridge crossing it near the upper half. But the bridge deck is not a normal roadway: it is a long air-raid siren horn spanning bank to bank, unmistakably a bridge in plan view with approaches meeting both shores. At the exact centre, a jagged red strike has just blown a chunk out of the siren-bridge, with debris breaking away over the water; keep the lower third mostly empty river so type can sit quietly.
art.note: Severe and tense, with cold greys, river blue, and one sharp burst of orange.
art.second_beat: First you see a bridge hit during an attack; a beat later you realise the bridge itself has become an air-raid siren, so the city’s vital connection is also the warning of its own destruction.

stories.headline: Storm in Catalonia kills two and triggers river flood alerts
stories.dek: A 75-year-old man died in Tordera, another person was found dead in Montornès, and crews are still searching near Pineda de Mar.
paragraphs: Severe weekend storms in Catalonia have killed two people, left one person missing and forced emergency alerts over rising rivers and flash floods. Authorities issued mobile warnings on Sunday as water levels surged in Barcelona's outskirts, the Maresme coast and parts of Girona province after torrential overnight rain.

One victim, a 75-year-old man, died in Tordera when a wall collapsed in a caravan area. Another person was found dead in Montornès del Vallès after going to a garage to get a car. Fire crews said they had rescued about 130 people from flooded basements and vehicles.

The main uncertainty is how high the rivers will rise and whether the missing person near the Pineda de Mar stream can be found. Officials warned people to stay away from the Besòs, Ridaura and Daró rivers, while some mobility limits remained in force and power outages were still being repaired.
stories.changes: If you live in or travel through northeast Catalonia, local movement, rail access and ground-floor safety may change quickly with phone alerts.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all of Catalonia is shut down, and some counties have already had movement restrictions lifted.

cover.title: Storm in Catalonia kills two as rivers rise
cover.standfirst: Weekend storms in Catalonia killed two people in Tordera and Montornès del Vallès, and one person is missing near Pineda de Mar. Authorities sent phone alerts for flood risk on Sunday as the Besòs, Ridaura and Daró rivers rose, while firefighters carried out about 130 rescues.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: A close, specific view of a caravan pitch in Tordera split by a hard vertical seam into two moments of the same place. On the left: the retaining wall stands intact beside the caravan, dry ground tight with severe engraved hatching; on the right: that same wall has just failed, white masonry blocks shearing downward into a black rush of floodwater that is forcing under the caravan chassis. Keep the caravan wheel and axle at exactly the same height on both sides so the eye measures the instant of collapse; no people, no extra scenery, and leave the lower third mostly open water and pale ground for type.
art.note: Silent, heavy mood; cold grey-blue and brown palette.
art.second_beat: First you read a simple split scene; a beat later the unchanged caravan wheel makes you realise this is the same exact spot at the moment the wall gives way.

stories.headline: Kulbergs party wins Latvian vote on pro-Ukraine platform
stories.dek: United List took 36.6% with most ballots counted, beating polls and putting defense spending and Ukraine aid at the center.
paragraphs: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List won Latvia’s parliamentary election, taking 36.6% of the vote with 88% of ballots counted. The result was stronger than polls had suggested. It gives Kulbergs a clear public mandate to keep high defense spending and continue military aid to Ukraine.

Latvia is a Baltic state of 1.9 million people on Russia’s and Belarus’s border and a member of NATO and the European Union. Security dominated the campaign. Kulbergs came to office in May after the last coalition fell apart over failures to detect stray military drones entering Latvian airspace.

The win does not give United List a majority in the 100-seat Saeima, so coalition talks must now begin. Kulbergs has said he does not want to govern with the populist Latvia First party. It is also not yet clear which smaller parties will back his budget, defense plans, and domestic spending promises.
stories.changes: Latvia is likely to keep backing Ukraine strongly and keep defense spending near the top of NATO.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Latvia can govern alone without compromise, or that any immediate security situation on the ground has changed.

cover.title: Kulbergs party wins Latvian election on support for Ukraine
cover.standfirst: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List won 36.6% of the vote in Latvia with 88% of ballots counted on Saturday, well ahead of rivals. The result supports his plan to keep defense spending at 5% of GDP and continue military aid to Ukraine, but he still needs coalition partners to govern.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: On a clean off-white field, a single ballot paper is folded into a recognisable fighter-interceptor shape and caught mid-launch, climbing diagonally upward from lower left to upper right as if just thrown by hand. Keep the creases, ballot-box checkbox grid, and paper weight unmistakable so it reads first as a vote; add only a few minimal motion lines and a small dark drone-like intruder shape ahead of its path near the upper edge, so the ballot is clearly becoming Latvia’s air defence without any words.
art.note: Firm public mood, crisp shapes, red, white, slate gray, and muted blue-yellow accents.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a democratic act in motion; a beat later the same ballot becomes a NATO-era interceptor answering the region’s drone-and-security threat.

stories.headline: Supreme Court opens term with climate, religion and gun cases
stories.dek: The justices begin Monday with a Colorado climate lawsuit that could shape where similar cases are heard across the country.
paragraphs: The Supreme Court starts its new term Monday with major disputes on climate change, religion, immigration and gun rights. The first argument is a Colorado case over whether Boulder can sue Exxon Mobil and Suncor in state court for local climate harms.

The case does not ask the court to decide who caused climate change. It asks where these lawsuits belong. Boulder says state law lets it seek damages for local costs. The energy companies say climate policy is national and cannot be set through many state courts.

Much remains undecided. The justices could limit or allow similar climate suits in other states. They will also hear a Colorado case on a Catholic preschool's access to public funding. More disputes tied to President Trump's agenda may reach the court later.

cover.title: Supreme Court opens term with climate, religion and gun cases
cover.standfirst: The justices begin Monday with a Colorado climate lawsuit that could shape where similar cases are heard across the country.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Build the cover from a rigid fence of identical black courthouse columns marching horizontally across an acid-green field, cropped so they feel institutional and endless. Near center, one column has been violently knocked sideways out of line, leaving a clean white gap; through that gap, and only there, a jagged black silhouette of refinery stacks and pipework intrudes from behind, unmistakably industrial. Keep the lower third largely open acid-green for type, with the fallen column and the refinery wedge sitting above it so the breach reads instantly and then deepens.
art.second_beat: First you see the Supreme Court as a sealed institutional wall; a beat later the missing column turns that wall into a jurisdictional breach, revealing the climate industry case suddenly visible through the opening.

stories.headline: UN says Ukraine civilian casualties rose 55 percent in 2026
stories.dek: The UN verified 15,280 civilian casualties in the first eight months, with guided bomb casualties nearing 2,500.
paragraphs: The United Nations said civilian casualties in Ukraine rose sharply in the first eight months of 2026. UN human rights chief Volker Türk told the Human Rights Council that 15,280 civilians were killed or wounded, up 55 percent from the same period in 2025. He gave the update in Geneva.

Türk said the increase came despite front lines changing little. He said Russian forces kept striking apartment blocks, schools, clinics, shops, railways, and energy sites. The UN said guided bomb attacks killed or wounded nearly 2,500 civilians, up 62 percent, with heavy use in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia.

The report also described wider abuse that is still not resolved. The UN said Russian forces and security services were responsible for 89 percent of more than 1,000 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence since 2022. It remains unclear whether the fighting will ease or whether civilian protection will improve soon.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the war is still causing rising harm far from the front and basic services remain at risk.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the front has suddenly collapsed or that the war's military balance changed overnight.

cover.title: UN says civilian casualties in Ukraine rose 55 percent
cover.standfirst: The United Nations says 15,280 civilians were killed or wounded in Ukraine in the first eight months of 2026. In Geneva, Volker Türk said guided bomb casualties rose to nearly 2,500 and said Russian forces were responsible for most verified sexual violence cases. The UN is urging stronger civilian protection.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Inside a modest Ukrainian kitchen, a breakfast table sits close to a cracked wall and window: bowl, mug, spoon, a child’s exercise book, all rendered in still engraved detail. Fine plaster dust is actively raining from above into the tea and across the page, a bare bulb swings slightly, and a fresh crack is visibly lengthening diagonally down the wall; one chair is skewed back and one place setting has been abruptly cleared, leaving a clean oval amid the settling dust. Keep the lower third quiet with the tabletop and floor so type can sit there easily.
art.note: Silent and severe, in ash gray, smoke black, and a muted rust red.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a tense domestic interior under bombardment; then you notice the clean gap where a child has just been snatched away a split second before the ceiling gives more.

stories.headline: UAE sent Israel FlyDubai crew details before foiled cockpit attack
stories.dek: Officials said Israel received the crew list, including nationalities, before the Tel Aviv flight where an Omani co-pilot attacked the captain.
paragraphs: Regional officials said the United Arab Emirates shared the FlyDubai flight's passenger and crew details with Israel before Wednesday's attempted cockpit takeover. That matters now because investigators are trying to explain how an Omani co-pilot with known extremist concerns boarded an Israel-bound flight undetected.

The co-pilot allegedly attacked the Indian captain with the cockpit crash ax and tried to seize control of the plane carrying 182 people to Tel Aviv. Passengers helped stop him after the captain opened the cockpit door. Israel and the UAE have security arrangements for flights between the two countries.

It is still unclear which authority should have flagged the pilot, why he was assigned to an Israel route, and what information was actually checked. Israeli agencies are blaming each other. Questions also remain about FlyDubai's screening and about limits on sharing security records across borders.
stories.changes: Airline crew vetting, not just passenger screening, is now likely to face closer checks on flights into Israel.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all UAE-Israel flights are unsafe or that ordinary passengers must expect cockpit attacks.

cover.title: UAE sent Israel FlyDubai crew details before cockpit attack
cover.standfirst: Officials said the UAE gave Israel the passenger and crew list before a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday. The plane carried 182 people when an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain with a crash ax. Investigators are now examining how he passed screening and was cleared for the route.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat hazard-orange ground, run a tight diagonal procession of stark black oval ID portraits, like crew/passport headshots clipped from a manifest, marching up and out of frame. Every oval contains the same blunt photocopy-style face except one near the front: inside that identical oval sits a solid black crash-ax head angled forward, and a single frantic marker circle/arrow snaps onto it as the late discovery; keep the entire lower third empty orange for type.
art.note: Sharp, tense collage in off-white, airline blue, black, and one hard red accent.
art.second_beat: First you see routine identity screening; a beat later you realize the weapon was already disguised inside the approved crew-list format.

stories.headline: Brazil prepares for a Lula and Bolsonaro election rematch
stories.dek: The 2026 presidential race is taking shape around a left-right contest with high stakes for Brazil and the wider region.
paragraphs: Brazil is heading toward a 2026 presidential contest centered on President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. The race matters now because both camps are already framing it as a choice about the country’s direction after years of sharp political division.

Lula is the leftist incumbent and one of Brazil’s best-known political figures. Flávio Bolsonaro carries the family name of the country’s recent right-wing movement. Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy and population center, so its elections often shape trade, diplomacy, climate policy and regional politics.

Much is still unsettled. Campaign rules, alliances, economic conditions and court decisions could all affect the field before voting begins. It is also unclear which issues will dominate voters’ choices, how broad each candidate’s support will be, and whether other contenders can break the two-sided contest.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this starts a long campaign that could affect Brazil’s economy, public policy and its role in Latin America.
stories.unchanged: It does not change Brazil’s government today, and early race framing does not mean the final ballot or result is settled.

cover.title: Brazil heads toward a Lula and Bolsonaro election rematch
cover.standfirst: Brazil’s 2026 presidential race is forming around incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. The contest will help decide the course of Latin America’s largest country, but alliances, court rulings and the economy could still reshape the field before voting.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a flat, saturated yellow seamless, place a Brazilian electronic voting machine three-quarters to camera, low and close, with a clean zipper seam forced straight down its middle and caught mid-open. From the opening, a small, controlled spill is actively tumbling out onto the surface: one unmistakable soyabean, a compact black fuel-nozzle tip, a green folded map with the Amazon basin silhouette visible by shape alone, and a plain bank card with chip but no text; keep the spill in the upper two-thirds so the lower third stays clear for type. Light it deadpan and precise so the machine remains instantly recognisable, but the impossible unzipping is the whole joke and argument.
art.note: Tense, public mood; red, green, yellow and off-white.
art.second_beat: First you see the ballot box behaving impossibly; a beat later you realise it is spilling out the ordinary sectors—agribusiness, fuel, the Amazon and money—that this rematch will materially reshape.

stories.headline: Trump puts intelligence chief Jay Clayton in charge of AI policy
stories.dek: Clayton will lead a White House task force with 120 days to report on AI risks, opportunities and federal responsibilities.
paragraphs: President Donald Trump has picked Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to lead the administration's artificial intelligence policy. Clayton will head a new White House task force that has 120 days to study AI risks and opportunities and recommend what the federal government should do next.

Clayton is a former Securities and Exchange Commission chair and former U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. The Senate confirmed him as director of national intelligence in July, putting him over 18 intelligence agencies. The White House calls the new group the Super Intelligence Force, or SI.

It is still unclear how much power Clayton will have beyond writing recommendations, and whether Trump will accept new federal rules. Trump has said he does not want to slow the industry, even as major AI companies and executives have asked for guardrails on advanced systems.
stories.changes: AI policy in Washington will now be shaped more directly through the White House and the intelligence system.
stories.unchanged: This does not create new AI rules yet, and it does not immediately change the tools people use at work or home.

cover.title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton to lead AI policy
cover.standfirst: President Donald Trump has chosen Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to run a new White House AI task force. The group has 120 days to report on risks, opportunities and the federal role, after recent White House talks with leading AI companies over voluntary safety standards.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: Show a vast, nearly empty field with the White House reduced to a small, unmistakable silhouette pushed slightly off-centre, leaving the lower third clear. Its central door is caught mid-swing open, but the door itself is cut in the profile of a human head — unmistakably a head-shaped slab rotating on hinges into the building. Keep everything else stripped away: no extra symbols, no text, just the precise moment intelligence is entering federal power but has not yet crossed the threshold.
art.note: Controlled, official mood; muted red, navy and machine gray.
art.second_beat: First you see the White House door opening; a beat later you realise the door is literally a human head, so AI policy is only at the point of entry into government, not yet inside.

stories.headline: Congo enrolls 250 people in Ebola prevention drug trial
stories.dek: The study tests an antiviral pill for people exposed to Bundibugyo Ebola within five days, before any symptoms begin.
paragraphs: Doctors in eastern Congo have enrolled more than 250 people in a trial of an experimental drug meant to stop Ebola after exposure. The study began in July during the country's worst recorded Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak. Researchers say it is a needed option because no approved vaccine or treatment exists for this strain.

The trial is testing obeldesivir, an antiviral pill made by Gilead. It is given to people who had recent contact with a confirmed Ebola case, including health workers and relatives. Participants must have no symptoms and must enroll within five days. Half receive the drug and half receive a placebo, with daily follow-up for 21 days.

It is still unknown whether the pill can prevent illness or slow spread enough to break chains of infection. Contact tracing remains hard, especially in remote areas, and some participants drop out after family deaths. Congo has recorded about 8,300 confirmed cases and 4,000 deaths since mid-May, while other vaccine studies also continue.
stories.changes: For people near an Ebola outbreak, this points to a possible treatment option after exposure, not just waiting to see if symptoms start.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Congo has a proven new Ebola cure or that the outbreak is under control.

cover.title: Congo tests Ebola pill on people exposed to the virus
cover.standfirst: More than 250 people in eastern Congo have joined a trial of an experimental antiviral pill aimed at preventing Bundibugyo Ebola after exposure. The study started in July and plans to enroll nearly 1,000 people, while the outbreak has already caused about 8,300 confirmed cases and 4,000 deaths.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: Top-down tabletop on a clinic-blue card ground, with the lower third left almost empty for type. A single fuzzy pipe-cleaner loop runs across the frame as one continuous contact ring shown in two states: on the left it cinches tight around a small red Ebola droplet, while on the right that same loop has just been snipped and the two cut ends spring backward, opening a gap. Three or four tiny white antiviral pills are caught mid-roll through the new opening toward the right, so the action is unmistakably post-exposure prevention — a transmission circle broken before illness begins.
art.note: Calm, clinical mood; soft earth tones with clean medical whites and pale blue.
art.second_beat: First you see a simple broken ring; a beat later you realise it is the same contact-tracing circle before and after intervention, with the pills using the cut to stop the chain.

stories.headline: Highway crash in Kenya kills 17 Catholic pilgrims
stories.dek: Police said a truck failed to overtake safely after midnight and hit several vehicles, including a van carrying pilgrims to a prayer site.
paragraphs: A multi-vehicle crash on the highway toward Mombasa killed 17 people in Kenya early Saturday, according to police. Most were Catholic pilgrims traveling in a van to a prayer site in Nakuru County. Police said the crash began when a truck driver tried to overtake another truck and failed.

The dead included the van driver and 16 passengers, most of them women, who died at the scene. The Salama stretch where the crash happened has been identified by Kenya's transport authority as a dangerous black spot. Road deaths in Kenya are often linked to speeding, unsafe overtaking, weak vehicle maintenance and poor road conditions.

It is not yet clear whether anyone else in the other vehicles was seriously injured or whether arrests will follow. Officials have not said when the victims will be buried. The transport authority says safety recommendations for this stretch had already been made, but it is unclear which measures, if any, were carried out.
stories.changes: For ordinary travelers in Kenya, this is another warning that some major highways remain dangerous, especially at night and on known crash stretches.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean all pilgrim travel or all roads to Mombasa are shut down or unusually unsafe today.

cover.title: Kenya highway crash kills 17 pilgrims traveling to prayer site
cover.standfirst: Seventeen people, mostly Catholic pilgrims, died after a truck tried to overtake another vehicle and hit several vehicles on a highway in Kenya after midnight Saturday. The pilgrims were traveling in a van to a prayer site in Nakuru County. Officials say the Salama stretch is a known danger spot.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Before sunrise at a rural Catholic prayer site in Nakuru County, set a simple outdoor altar and neat rows of plastic chairs on dusty ground, with the lower third kept mostly bare earth for type. Over many chair backs, white veils and shawls are draped and caught by a gust so they lift and half-peel away at once; beside the altar, a food pot still gives off steam near stacked yellow jerrycans, making it unmistakably a reception prepared for arriving pilgrims who never came.
art.note: Somber and spare, with charcoal blacks, dim amber headlights, and muted gray-blue road tones.
art.second_beat: First you see a waiting worship site; then you realise the 'congregation' is only garments on empty chairs, so the absence becomes the story.
